newsitem.title: JAPAN: Saudi price cut to Asia seen hitting W.African oil.
newsitem.headline: Saudi price cut to Asia seen hitting W.African oil.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's decision to slash the August term price for Arab Light by 40 cents a barrel may reflect the major oil producer's concern over the steady flow of West African barrels into Asia, traders said on Friday.
The deep cut took Asian traders by surprise on Thursday, with one trader labelling the sharp reduction "unbelievable".
"I think Saudi Arabia was alarmed at the flow of West African cargoes reaching Asia," an oil company trader said.
Some Gulf and Asian crudes have suffered weak demand in recent weeks because of the major presence of West African material in Asia.

Because Saudi Arabia values its grades based on a differential to the average of Oman and Dubai grades, the sharp Saudi reduction puts immediate downward pressure on Asia's leading benchmark Dubai grade. Tokyo traders said a lower Dubai value would help widen the recently narrow Brent/Dubai differential, which is the main trigger for West African flows east.

A lower Dubai value relative to North Sea benchmark Brent, means that Dubai-linked crudes become more attractive than their Brent-linked counterparts. Already, Dubai's discount to Brent (the Brent/Dubai spread) has widened to about $1.25/$1.30, compared to levels last week of just $1.00, which traders say will likely see a reduction in the flow east of Brent-related West African barrels.
Buyers said the price cut, which valued August loading Arab Light on a par with the Oman/Dubai value, would likely cut into sales of Dubai and Oman as well.
"Given a choice between buying Arab Light and Dubai, we would buy the Saudi crude," said one trader with a Japanese refiner.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia lowered its August lifting price formula for Arab light to parity with the Oman/Dubai average, down 40 cents from the July formula.
Tokyo traders said they did not believe Arab Light's official selling price had ever been at parity or at a discount with the Oman/Dubai value.
Saudi Arabia also cut the August term price of its Berri Extra Light grade by 50 cents and its Arab Super Light grade by 60 cents. Arab Medium was reduced by 10 cents, and Arab Heavy was rolled over.
Analysts say 1997 crude cargoes from West Africa to Asia already average some 770,000 barrels per day (bpd) through May.
The figure marks a 30.4 percent jump over the 590,000 bpd level seen in the first five months of 1996.
The largest volume of purchases has been made by South Korea, with 22.6 percent of total Asian buying, according to the London-based research team of tanker broker Simpson, Spence and Young.
